name: Karl Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and a junior developer on a water-billing portal for a tech company. I used to read meters in the field and took a two-year college diploma to work on the screens, but I still need my supervisor to review the code. My wife Maren works as a teaching assistant, and we have a mortgage and two school-age children; I like matching a bill to a real reading before anyone is charged wrongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI may sort routine meter reports, but a customer still needs a correct bill and a number to call. I use the tool occasionally to explain code, then compare the answer with the meter reading myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior pay is ordinary for this job, and we have about five months of basic expenses saved. My wife Maren is a teaching assistant, so we can cover the mortgage and our two children while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing the water-billing portal and ask the field desk to send me one disputed reading each week. We would keep putting 90 monthly into the roof repair account if both pay cheques arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about the next year. I still have a lot to learn, but a small tool does not change the bills we already know how to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do before software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I read water meters in the field, then took a two-year college diploma so I could help fix the billing screens. I am 43 and a junior software developer, but I know what a muddy meter box looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a roof account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A corner of the roof leaked last winter, and we paid for a patch. I want the next repair to come from cash, not a new loan.

I compare occasional **AI answers** with actual meter figures.
think: I have **five months saved** and ordinary junior pay.
I see two continuing wages covering our **mortgage and children** for now.
do: **Keep fixing** water-billing screens and review a disputed reading weekly.
**Save 90 monthly** for roof repairs if both wages continue.
feel: **Calm** about the next year, despite skills still to learn.

fieldNote: His prior **field meter work** helps him test a billing screen against real readings.
Two wages and **five months saved** support calm while the household funds roof repairs.

steps.text: Keep fixing water-billing screens and review disputed meter readings
Save 90 monthly for roof repairs while both wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that AI can write the routine billing fixes I still get assigned. I would ask the supervisor to show us which jobs change and how an incorrect bill will be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could shrink before the senior developer’s, and a five-month cushion has to serve the whole family. Maren’s school pay cannot cover the mortgage and roof work alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask a colleague to show me an AI check for a meter reading that jumps too high, then practise with fake accounts if my supervisor allows it on paid time. In the first year I’d ask about paid field-meter vacancies if developer hours are cut, and I would not leave until an offer covers the mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious and somewhat annoyed. I can learn when the tool proves itself, but I have spent years learning water meters and billing code that the firm may now buy more cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the AI check works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d give it three old readings where a digit was entered twice. If it flags the wrong household, it is not ready for a customer bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the field job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever; robots spread more slowly into hands-on work, and I would watch that. I have done the field route before, so a paid opening might carry us through the first change.

think: I expect my **junior hours** could shrink before senior roles.
I know Maren’s **school pay** cannot cover the mortgage alone.
do: **Learn AI meter checks** on fake accounts only if paid practice is approved.
**Ask about field jobs** if developer hours are cut; move only for bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and the cost of replacing skilled work.
S1.quote: I have spent years learning water meters and billing code that the firm may now buy more cheaply.
fieldNote: His **field background** offers a possible paid move, but robots later threaten hands-on work.
He requires **proof on fake readings** and approved paid time before trying the AI check.

steps.text: Practise an AI high-meter-reading check only with paid supervisor approval

Accept only field offers covering mortgage and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could do nearly all the code and bill checking I now learn from. Robots for field work might arrive around 2031, so a meter route is only a temporary shelter if it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior developer role could end even though I know the field side. Five months saved could carry a search, but not the mortgage forever, and Maren would still need help with the children after school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the supervisor now for a written date and pay terms if developer roles are cut. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am displaced, I’d apply for paid meter-service vacancies only if they exist and cover our bills; we would put the roof repair on hold unless a leak returned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, but I would know where to start looking. The field route could pay the mortgage for a while, not erase the 2031 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we still keep the house dry, but the bigger repair must wait while I search for work. I would not spend their school fund on a roof that has stopped leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a short field contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the rate covers the mortgage and we know when it ends. I would use the time to keep applying, because a temporary route is not a pension.

say: I say **thinking AGI in 2028** reaches my code before field robots arrive.
I would call **meter service** a temporary paid option, not a permanent shelter.
think: I expect my **junior role** might end despite field experience.
I know **five months saved** cannot cover the mortgage indefinitely.
do: **Request a written date** and pay terms for developer cuts from my supervisor now.
**Apply for meter work** only if displaced after 2028 and offers cover bills.
**Delay the roof repair** unless the leak returns, keeping the school fund intact.
feel: **Alarmed**, but clear on a short-term field option.
S2.quote: The field route could pay the mortgage for a while, not erase the 2031 robot date.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year robot lag** as temporary time for a hands-on role.
The **roof decision** protects children’s school money while keeping urgent leak repairs possible.

steps.text: Apply for paid meter-service vacancies if displaced after 2028
Accept only meter-service offers that cover mortgage and basic bills
Delay larger roof repairs unless the leak returns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 lets us fix the billing mistakes we already know about. Robots for meter routes might follow around 2034, so I would not tell field staff they are safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become a stronger developer by learning from disputed bills, but AI may do that thinking work in 2031. We can also build more roof cash if both wages stay steady, so a job loss need not become a roof loan straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my supervisor for a monthly review on paid time of one disputed bill, including the meter photo and corrected amount, and do it only if approved. I’d put 140 monthly in the roof account if both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d seek paid customer-meter work only where posts remain and pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but less hurried. I want my water-meter experience to count for something, even if it cannot beat a machine forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from a dispute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check whether the wrong number came from the field reading, a copied digit, or my code. My supervisor could tell me which part of my fix still needs work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; the roof and mortgage need cash. I would learn from the disputed bills on paid time and consider a course only if the company paid for it.

He protects **roof cash** and mortgage payments while testing paid field options, knowing a job loss could make a roof loan difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives the water company time to teach people how bills and meters fit together. Robots might handle field readings around 2039, after AI has already changed the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but the roof and mortgage may still be ours to pay. I could build a six-month cushion and learn a practical repair skill before 2036, though robots may eventually reach that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the billing portal and spend about 180 from our five-month cushion on an evening plumbing-basics class, but only if Maren agrees, the roof stays dry and the mortgage reserve remains intact. I’d attend the six-week class and practise safe household repairs; separately, we’d save 120 monthly if both wages continue. If my developer job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid water-service vacancies only where they still exist and the pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, with time to learn something I can touch. I would not tell the children a short class guarantees a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the class let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might spot a leak or replace a simple tap at home after learning the safety rules. I would not call myself a plumber or take paid jobs without proper training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use savings for the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five months saved lets us pay 180 if the roof stays dry and Maren agrees. If the roof leaks again, the class waits and the repair money stays put.

say: I want **meter and bill skills** taught before full AGI reaches our code in 2036.
I know **field robots around 2039** follow the thinking-work change.
think: I could build a **six-month cushion** and learn a practical repair skill.
I know **roof and mortgage costs** may remain even as the children grow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code work could go before a stable replacement exists. A paid meter-service offer that covers our mortgage, a written job date and time to keep the school fund intact would help; I know robots could reach field work around 2031.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask about the roof. A leak can turn a job gap into a new loan, so the roof account matters alongside the mortgage.

headlineQuote: A leak can turn a job gap into a new loan, so the roof account matters alongside the mortgage.
portrait: Karl is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, ordinary pay and five months of expenses saved.
He and Maren support **two children** and a mortgage while saving for roof repairs.
His old **meter-reading work** helps him check billing code, and he tries AI occasionally after proof.
The **2028 scenario** threatens his screen job; field meter work might pay only until robots reach it later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer wage before a lasting replacement is clear.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date**, bill-covering meter-service offer and protected school money would help during the search.
